rationale: Tryphon's projected invasion gives concrete form to the surrounding nations' announced plan to crush Israel after Jonathan's capture.
The people's terror continues the fear and mourning that accompanied the survivors' return after Jonathan was captured.
Simon's appeal to his family's sacrifices for the law recalls Mattathias's charge to his sons to give their lives for the ancestral covenant.
Judas's death in battle supplies one of the fraternal losses recalled in Simon's declaration; it does not resolve the speech's anticipation of Jonathan's death, narrated later in chapter 13.
Eleazar's death beneath the elephant is a particular instance of the brothers' deaths for Israel recalled by Simon.
Simon's refusal to spare his own life continues his father's express command that his sons give their lives for the covenant.
Simon's promise to defend the nation answers the surrounding nations' explicit plan to destroy a people they believe now lacks a leader.
The people's choice of Simon in place of Judas and Jonathan repeats the earlier communal choice of Jonathan to replace Judas as leader.
The request that Simon fight their war repeats the task explicitly assigned to Jonathan when the people chose him as ruler and leader.
Simon's urgent completion of Jerusalem's walls continues the rebuilding program Jonathan and the elders had begun.
The renewed deployment to Joppa consolidates Simon's earlier seizure and garrisoning of the city against its proposed surrender to Demetrius's men.
Jonathan's guarded presence with Tryphon follows his seizure at Ptolemais, where his accompanying men were killed.
Simon's encampment at Adida uses the stronghold he had recently rebuilt and fortified in the Shephelah.
The demand for Jonathan's sons and one hundred talents promises his release; the later report records delivery of both and Tryphon's refusal to release him.
The payment and delivery of the sons fulfil the exact ransom conditions, exposing Tryphon's breach of his promise to release Jonathan.
Tryphon's invasion implements the surrounding enemies' plan to crush Israel, while Simon's counter-movement supplies the leadership they had assumed absent.
The citadel's request for food follows Jonathan's plan to isolate it so that its inhabitants could neither buy nor sell.
Tryphon's killing of Jonathan brings to completion the earlier stated intention to seize and destroy him because he might oppose Tryphon's kingship.
Simon brings Jonathan to the ancestral burial place at Modein, where he and Jonathan had previously buried Judas.
Israel's great lament and many days of mourning for Jonathan repeat the wording and duration of the national mourning for Judas.
The monumental tomb is built over the family burial place in Modein where Mattathias had been buried.
The opening family list identifies Mattathias and his five sons, including Simon and the four brothers commemorated here; it does not name their mother or describe the pyramids.
The armour memorials seek an everlasting name for the family, echoing the stated aim of Simon's brother Eleazar when he gave himself to save the people.
The enduring monument in Modein marks the same ancestral burial site to which Simon and Jonathan had brought Judas.
Tryphon's killing of the young Antiochus carries out his earlier intention to attack the king and claim the diadem.
Tryphon's assumption of the diadem of Asia realizes the precise royal ambition stated before his seizure of Jonathan.
Simon's rebuilding and provisioning of Judea's strongholds implements the stronghold program previously considered by Jonathan and the elders.
Simon's mission seeking remission renews the earlier negotiation in which Jonathan obtained Demetrius's written agreement to free Judea and associated districts from tribute.
The later public inscription recalls Demetrius's confirmation of Simon's high priesthood and status as Friend, both titles used in this royal greeting.
Demetrius's promise to instruct his officials about remissions continues the earlier written grant relinquishing royal dues and crown payments.
Royal recognition that the built strongholds belong to the Jews concerns the defensive works previously undertaken at Jerusalem and Adida.
The removal of crown payments renews the earlier royal grant that explicitly relinquished those payments along with other dues.
The invitation to enrol suitable Jews in royal service resembles the earlier Demetrius's offer of paid enrolment and trusted appointments; these are distinct royal offers, not a single decree.
The removal of the nations' yoke realizes the stated objective for which Judas had earlier sought an alliance with Rome.
The dating of documents in Simon's name corresponds to the public decree requiring all documents in the country to be written in his name.
The inscription's account of Simon's restoration and Jewish settlement of Gazara presupposes the capture narrated here.
The city's appeal for Simon's right hand repeats the concrete diplomatic gesture requested by the defeated people of Antioch before they laid down their weapons and made peace.

The plea not to be treated according to wickedness but with mercy resembles the psalm's statement that the Lord has not dealt with His people according to their sins; the petition here is addressed to Simon.
The expulsion of Gazara's inhabitants and cleansing of its houses underlie the inscription's account of replacing the city's former enemies with Jewish settlers.
The law-observant settlement and fortification of Gazara are the particular works later commemorated in the public inscription.
The citadel's inability to buy and sell, ending in famine, fulfils the stated purpose of Jonathan's barrier separating it from the city.
The expulsion and cleansing of the citadel reverse its establishment as a foreign stronghold whose occupants shed blood and defiled the sanctuary.
The joyful entry with hymns, lyres, harps, and cymbals resembles the musical celebration of the sanctuary's rededication; the citadel victory has its own date and occasion.
The institution of an annual joyful anniversary repeats the earlier decision to commemorate the altar's dedication each year, while establishing a distinct observance.
John's later report to his father from Gazara follows his appointment as military commander and residence in that city.
Demetrius seeks eastern aid against Tryphon after Tryphon's usurpation and Simon's appeal to Demetrius against his plundering rule.
Judah's quiet throughout Simon's days recalls the description of security throughout Solomon's days in the Greek-numbered Kings passage.
The praise of Simon's acquisition of Joppa recalls his seizure and garrisoning of the city; the present summary adds its value as a harbour.
The expansion praised here is later defended by Simon as recovery of ancestral inheritance when the king contests Jewish control.
The summary's possession of Beth-zur recalls Simon's blockade, negotiated surrender, expulsion of the occupants, and installation of a garrison there.
The possession and purification of Gazara and the citadel summarize the preceding accounts of their surrender, expulsion of former occupants, and cleansing.
Peaceful cultivation, the land yielding produce, and the trees yielding fruit reproduce the specific agricultural and security blessings attached to obedience in Leviticus.
The elders seated in the squares recall Zechariah's vision of old people sitting safely in Jerusalem's squares; the young men's military splendour differs from the prophet's playing children.
The praise of food supplies and city defences recalls Simon's specific work of fortifying Judea and storing food in its strongholds.

Within Simon's portrait of fruitful land (14:8) and life without fear (14:12), peace upon the land recalls Leviticus's linked blessings of peace and freedom from terror. This is covenant imagery, without identifying Simon's rule as an exhaustive fulfilment.
Each person beneath vine and fig tree with none causing fear closely reproduces Micah's image of secure life; the comparison does not identify Simon's reign with every part of Micah's future vision.
The vine-and-fig-tree description also recalls the security of Judah and Israel throughout Solomon's reign, preserved here under the Greek verse label 2:46g.
Simon's removal of lawless persons continues the specific judicial policy attributed to Jonathan when he settled at Michmash and removed the ungodly from Israel.
Simon's multiplication of sacred vessels continues the restoration begun when Judas rebuilt the holy places and supplied new vessels.
The news that grieves Rome and Sparta concerns Jonathan's killing at Bascama, narrated in the preceding chapter.
Foreign recognition of Simon's succession follows the people's choice of him as leader in place of Judas and Jonathan.
The renewal explicitly recalls the friendship established under Judas, whose envoys obtained a Roman agreement recorded on bronze tablets.
The friendship associated with Jonathan recalls his dispatch of envoys to Rome to renew the existing alliance.

The Spartans address the Jewish people as brothers, using the brotherhood language of Jonathan's earlier letter. The later letter addresses Simon, so the shared language establishes diplomatic continuity without proving it is a reply to that particular letter.

The Spartan acknowledgment of Jewish envoys continues the diplomacy attested by Jonathan's commission to visit Sparta and deliver letters. The later correspondence addresses Simon; it does not unequivocally identify this arrival as that same journey.
Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason are the same named envoys Jonathan commissioned to renew friendship at Rome and then visit Sparta.

Jonathan requested an answer about renewed friendship, while the later Spartan decision records reception of envoys and sends Simon a copy. These passages document continued written correspondence, without establishing that the copy is the precise answer to Jonathan's request.
The Roman letter subsequently records the arrival and acceptance of the thousand-mina golden shield that Simon sends with Numenius here.
The inscription's praise of the family's resistance and freedom recalls Mattathias's successful campaign that took the law out of the nations' hands.
The public tribute to Simon's establishment of freedom commemorates the preceding declaration that the nations' yoke had been removed.
The inscription dates itself in Simon's third year, continuing the documentary era begun when the yoke was removed and contracts were first dated in his name.
The inscription identifies Simon as Mattathias's son from the priestly family of Joarib, the ancestry given when Mattathias first appears.
The brothers' exposure to danger for the law and holy places commemorates their father's charge to give their lives for the ancestral covenant.
The inscription's summary of Jonathan's high priesthood refers to his royal appointment and subsequent assumption of the holy robe.
Jonathan's being gathered to his people summarizes his killing, recovery for burial at Modein, and national mourning.
The inscription's threatened invasion recalls Tryphon's gathering of a large force to enter Judah and crush it.

The tribute to Simon's resistance recalls his refusal to spare his life, acceptance of leadership, and mobilization of the army; the earlier passage does not specify the pay or his personal expenditure.
The inscription's Jewish garrison at Beth-zur recalls Simon's capture of that city and replacement of its occupants with his own garrison.
The inscription's restoration of Joppa recalls Simon's earlier seizure of the city and installation of a protective garrison.
The restoration and Jewish settlement of Gazara repeat the specific account of its cleansing, law-observant settlers, and additional fortifications.
The inscription's appointment of Simon as leader recalls the people's acclamation and promise to obey him in their war; that earlier acclamation does not itself describe a priestly investiture.
The inscription identifies the foreign citadel in the city of David and its pollution of the sanctuary's surroundings, recalling the original account of its construction and violence.
The successful removal of the citadel's foreigners recalls its famine, negotiated surrender, expulsion, and cleansing under Simon.
The inscription's account of raised Jerusalem walls recalls Simon's urgent completion and strengthening of those walls.
Demetrius's confirmation of Simon's high priesthood is reflected in his letter addressing Simon explicitly as high priest.
The inscription's recognition of Simon as a royal Friend corresponds to the title Friend of kings used in Demetrius's greeting.
The Roman letter calls the Jews friends and allies and accepts their envoys' shield, documenting the recognition summarized here; its greeting does not supply the additional word brothers.
The settlement pending a faithful prophet recalls the earlier deferral of the altar-stone question until a prophet should give an answer.
Simon's appointment as national general extends the earlier royal appointment placing him over the coastal region from the Ladder of Tyre to Egypt.
The decree requiring documents in Simon's name corresponds to the dated contracts already reported at the beginning of his era.
Simon's right to purple and gold ornaments continues the specific royal privileges previously granted to Jonathan, his predecessor.
The prohibition on others wearing purple or a golden clasp reserves to Simon insignia earlier specifically authorized for Jonathan by the king.
The people's agreement to the formal settlement continues their earlier acclamation of Simon and promise to obey his command.
Simon's acceptance of priestly, military, and national leadership corresponds to the combined titles already used to date the people's contracts.
The order to display the bronze inscription conspicuously at the holy places follows the earlier instruction to exhibit Demetrius's grant conspicuously on the holy mountain.
Antiochus's address recognizes Simon as priest and ethnarch, the offices Simon accepted in the preceding public settlement.
Antiochus's claim that men have seized his ancestral kingdom responds to Tryphon's killing of the young king and assumption of the diadem.
The announced landing and pursuit are followed by Antiochus's entry into the land and pursuit of Tryphon to Dora.
Antiochus confirms prior remissions of the kind Demetrius explicitly granted Simon, including crown-payment remission and recognized possession of strongholds.
The guarantee that Jewish weapons and strongholds remain theirs renews Demetrius's explicit recognition of ownership of the strongholds they built.
The comprehensive cancellation of royal debts and future dues continues Demetrius's earlier cancellation of crown payments and levies in Jerusalem.
The promised future honour is overturned when Antiochus rejects Simon's assistance, annuls his agreements, and becomes hostile.
Tryphon now loses his troops, contrasting with his earlier rise when the forces dismissed by Demetrius joined the young Antiochus he supported; the passages describe different changes of allegiance.
The blockade preventing entry and exit is explicitly resumed after the intervening Roman correspondence, again identifying Dora and Tryphon's confinement.
Numenius's return from Rome with letters completes the embassy Simon sent with the golden shield to establish the alliance.
Rome's statement that Simon's envoys came to renew the alliance reports the completion of the mission sent with Numenius.
The thousand-mina golden shield is the exact gift Simon entrusted to Numenius for the Roman mission.
Rome's prohibition on harming the Jews or supporting their enemies applies the protective obligations in the earlier Roman-Jewish alliance.
The Roman decision to accept the shield records the outcome of Simon's dispatch of that particular gift with Numenius.
After the inserted Roman letters, the narrative returns to the same siege of Dora and the earlier prohibition of entry and exit.
Simon's offer of two thousand men to Antiochus recalls Jonathan's dispatch of three thousand to help Demetrius; the kings, troop totals, and reception differ.
Antiochus's rejection of assistance and annulment of agreements reverse the particular remissions, property guarantees, and honours he had just promised Simon.
Antiochus's estrangement after an offer of help resembles Demetrius's earlier betrayal and estrangement from Jonathan after Jewish military assistance.
The royal demand names Joppa, Gazara, and the Jerusalem citadel, the same strategic possessions celebrated in the preceding summary of Simon's achievements.
The king denounces Jewish control of added territory as devastation, reversing the preceding praise of Simon's enlargement of the nation's borders.

Antiochus demands cities and revenue, contrasting with Demetrius's earlier recognition of Jewish strongholds and remission of Jerusalem levies. The demand here concerns places outside Judea, so the passages do not define identical territorial or tax terms.
The king's demand for two payments of five hundred talents receives Simon's much smaller counteroffer of one hundred talents for Joppa and Gazara.

Simon's denial of taking foreign land resembles Jephthah's reply to a demand for disputed territory: both reject the accusation and defend Israel's possession through its earlier history, without equating the territories.
Simon's resolve to retain ancestral inheritance resembles Jephthah's insistence that Israel retain what its God allotted it; Simon here stresses recovery when opportunity arose.
Simon addresses the named disputed cities and offers one hundred talents in response to the king's demand for their surrender or far larger compensation.
Tryphon's flight by ship escapes the land-and-sea blockade imposed after his earlier retreat to Dora; the target describes the confinement from which he now escapes.
The infantry and cavalry entrusted to Cendebaeus become the force that John confronts and routs in the next chapter.
The order to rebuild Kedron explains the later description of John pursuing the defeated enemy to Kedron, which Cendebaeus had built.
Cendebaeus's invasions, captures, and killings supply the actions John reports to his father before the Jewish counter-campaign.
Cendebaeus's rebuilding and garrisoning of Kedron establish the stronghold to which John subsequently pursues his defeated forces.
John comes from Gazara as the commander whom Simon had appointed and stationed there.
John's report concerns the preceding account of Cendebaeus's attacks on Judea and establishment of Kedron as a base for sorties.
Simon's final charge recalls his earlier appeal to the family's hardships and his own resolve to continue his brothers' service at risk of death.
An aged leader entrusting the nation's future fighting to successors with an appeal to divine help resembles Moses' commission of Joshua; Simon commissions two sons rather than one successor.
The charge to John and Judas develops Simon's earlier appointment of the now-grown John as commander of all the forces.
The expedition against Cendebaeus responds to his raids into Judea and establishment of a fortified base for further attacks.

John crosses the stream first and his men follow, closely repeating Judas's earlier advance across a watercourse before his men despite the danger of fear and hesitation; the opponents and battles differ.
The trumpet signal in defence against an invading adversary corresponds to the law's instruction to signal with trumpets when fighting enemies in Israel's land.
The text explicitly identifies Kedron as Cendebaeus's construction, referring back to his royal commission and execution of that work.

John's defeated enemies retreat into towers in Azotus's countryside before he burns 'it'; the earlier campaign also ends with flight to Azotus and burning, but explicitly names the city and Dagon's shrine. The refuges and casualty totals differ; the source's pronoun does not explicitly identify the towers as what burned.
Ptolemy's intention to remove Simon and his sons is carried out through the deceptive feast and armed murders subsequently narrated.
Ptolemy's drinking feast concealing assassins resembles Absalom's feast used to kill Amnon through waiting servants; the motives and victims remain distinct.
The killing after Simon and his sons become drunk resembles Absalom's express instruction to kill Amnon when his heart was merry with wine.
The narrator's judgment that Ptolemy repaid evil for good repeats the precise moral reversal condemned in the proverb, without asserting that its predicted household punishment is narrated here.
The dispatch of killers to John at Gazara is frustrated when a messenger warns him and he seizes and kills the men sent against him.
The warning that assassins have been sent tells John about the precise mission Ptolemy has just dispatched to Gazara.
John's execution of the men sent to kill him reverses Ptolemy's particular assassination mission against him at Gazara.
The summary of John's remaining wars and brave deeds resembles the earlier closing notice about Judas; Judas's many deeds are said to remain unwritten, whereas John's notice leads to a named record.
The referral to the book recording John's high priesthood resembles Kings' referral to the book of Solomon's acts for the remaining deeds; the offices, figures, and named records differ.
